items.title: 这周做了个大活，我在为 #vibench 设计 Coordinator 的核心逻辑以及 UI，这件事前后加起来花了我三天…

quote.text: 这周做了个大活，我在为 #vibench 设计 Coordinator 的核心逻辑以及 UI，这件事前后加起来花了我三天时间。Coordinator 的设计是我一直以来的想法，其根源来自于我的工作流程痛点所经历的三个时期的变化。 第一个时期，我做事情的每个步骤都要开会话，重复输入相似的 prompt。当时的流程是：先开一个 Plan Mode，把 Plan 写出来，然后再开一个会话去 Review Plan；完了之后再去执行，执行完有时候觉得结论不够充分，还要再开个会话做额外的验证。目前 vibench 已经实现了通过 Issue 去提前记录和安排工作，然后在 Issue 里面实现能够自动流转的多阶段会话，我只需要在阶段中间介入，点一点按钮它就可以进行到下一个阶段。 到了第二个时期，痛点在于多线工作时常会产生阻塞。比方说我正在做任务 A，这时候想去做任务 B，我虽然可以先规划 B，却没法直接执行，因为我知道必须等 A 做完再去执行 B 是最好的。如果让它们两个同时在 Master 上工作又会容易产生冲突；但如果改用 Worktree，一个任务做完之后，我又可能会忘了去合并它——毕竟 Worktree 要合回 Master，也得等 Master 上的任务跑完。所以要持续追踪各项任务当前的进度。后来这个问题也在 vibench 里解决了，我给 Issue 增加了 Worktree 支持和排队功能：都在 Master 上工作的 Issue 可以排队等待；在 Worktree 上工作的 Issue 则可以并行推进，等合并到 Master 时再排队，并且排完一个就会自动让下一个开始工作。 到了第三个时期，我开始规划较大规模的任务。一个大任务同时包含几个不同方向的事情，比如设计、前端、后端，可能还有跟其他服务的对接。用项目管理的话说，我的工作单位从 Issue 上升到了 Epic 的工作。这个时期我喜欢先做完整的规划，一个 plan 里会分好几期来实现。我写了一个 herdr-coordinator Skill，它会启动一个专门用来做协调而不做实际开发的会话，通过 Herdr 去开新的 Tab，调用适当的 Agent 去安排工作，并监督把握当前整体的进展情况，持续推进这个任务。有的时候一个任务的周期可能会持续一两天之久。 这个时期的痛点在于，这种工作方式会导致我很难去了解当前的全局进展。有的时候工作进行到中段，一开就是上十个 Tab，每个 Tab 跑的事情都不同。在 Herdr 里看着望不到头的 tabs，根本无法知道发生了什么。有的时候某一个 Tab 需要去介入而我不知道，很容易因此而 Block 了别的 tab 的进展，浪费很多时间。你得不断地在大脑里构建出一个图景：哪些事情大致在做？然后手动去关注、点击，以确保它能够更好地按照自己的意愿工作。我感觉玩 RTS 多个基地同时发展 + 微操战斗都没有这么累。我也尝试过跟 Coordinator 说：“你自己来想办法帮我去回答问题和推进，不要让我介入。”但是这样做效果明显比我自己掌舵要差，有的时候会绕很大的路。说白了，它还未能具备足够好的自动驾驶能力。可它也未能提供让我能舒服地掌控全局的界面以及便捷的操作工具。 因此我就一直在思考，要自己实现一个 Coordinator 的 Agent Loop 和界面。正好这时候 Personal Agent 开始出现，它带来的体验革命就是全双工的会话，实际上它们的设计架构都大差不差。用过一些产品的读者都知道，它的主会话界面是不会阻塞消息的，无论它此刻在后台运行什么，你都可…

LibreOffice – the suite – includes no AI features built in. It doesn’t try to change your content, share your data, or use your work to train models. If you want AI features, you can add them via extensions – but the software itself has zero AI features inside. Regarding software development: there are ongoing discussions about the use of large language models (LLMs) when working on source code. Some free and open source software (FOSS) projects have chosen to close contributions from the public altogether, while they work out how to handle LLM-assisted code submissions – effectively becoming “invite-only” clubs. We hope to never have to make such a drastic change. Avoiding any influence of AI-assisted coding tools in a large software project like LibreOffice is not possible. Security issue reports involve more and more use of LLMs, and refusing to acknowledge them would not benefit the software or our users. Our third party dependencies – and even the compilers we depend on – include AI-assisted code. We don’t want to reject any valuable code contributions that make the software better for everyone, just because an LLM was used at one point. But our focus is strongly on human-generated

LibreOffice – the suite – includes no AI features built in. It doesn’t try to change your content, share your data, or use your work to train models. If you want AI features, you can add them via extensions – but the software itself has zero AI features inside. Regarding software development: there are ongoing discussions about the use of large language models (LLMs) when working on source code. Some free and open source software (FOSS) projects have chosen to close contributions from the public altogether, while they work out how to handle LLM-assisted code submissions – effectively becoming “invite-only” clubs. We hope to never have to make such a drastic change. Avoiding any influence of AI-assisted coding tools in a large software project like LibreOffice is not possible. Security issue reports involve more and more use of LLMs, and refusing to acknowledge them would not benefit the software or our users. Our third party dependencies – and even the compilers we depend on – include AI-assisted code. items.summary: Planning a career in Linux, cloud or DevOps? LFCS, CKA, Kubestronaut and other Linux Foundation certifications are up to 65% off for Cyber Monday. Offer ends December 4.
items.body:
If you have been planning to get a certification, this is the week to do it. The Linux Foundation is running its Black Friday and Cyber Week sale, and you can get up to 65% off on certifications, bundles, training courses and the THRIVE-ONE e-learning subscription.

This is also a good gift idea. If you have a friend or family member who wants to build a career in Linux, cloud or DevOps, a certification exam is a more useful present than another gadget.

Getting certified could also be your new year resolution. Lock in the exam price today, and take the exam in 2027.

The offer ends on December 4, 2026 at 23:59 UTC. And this is the biggest discount that you won't see on other occasions.

Linux Foundation Cyber Week Offer

There is also a bonus this time. Everyone who buys with one of the promo codes before December 4 gets a $100 voucher that can be used on an e-learning course, instructor-led training or certification purchased between January 1 and October 31, 2027. The Linux Foundation will email the voucher details by December 31, 2026.

This article contains affiliate links. Please read our affiliate policy.

Your discount codes

Here are the codes. They are specific to It's FOSS readers, so use these and not the generic ones you see on the promo page.

So pretty much every certification in the Linux Foundation catalog is at least 50% off this week. That includes LFCS, CKA, CKAD, CKS and the brand new Certified Kubernetes Network Engineer (CKNE), all down from $445 to $223.

Even if the offer ends, you can always get 30% off with our special coupon code: ITSFOSS.

💡

Apply the code on the checkout page. The discount is for new, individual purchases only and cannot be combined with other offers.

Why a Linux Foundation certification carries weight

The Linux Foundation is the umbrella organization for some of the most important open source projects out there. It employs Linus Torvalds, the creator of Linux, so that he can work on the kernel full time. It is also the home of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), which in turn hosts Kubernetes, Prometheus, Argo and plenty of the other tools that run modern cloud infrastructure.

The foundation counts the biggest names in tech among its members: Google, Microsoft, IBM, Intel, Oracle, Red Hat and hundreds more. These are the same companies that hire people who run Linux servers and Kubernetes clusters.

So when the Linux Foundation offers a certification, it comes from the industry that builds these technologies. That is why recruiters recognize CKA or LFCS on a resume.

💡

65% off is the biggest discount Linux Foundation offers on Cyber Monday. You won't get a bigger discount than this on any other occassion.

Best picks for a Linux, cloud and DevOps career

There are over a hundred discounted products, and that can be overwhelming. If the goal is a job in Linux administration, cloud or DevOps, here are the ones worth considering.

LFCS Exam + THRIVE-ONE Annual: $625 $516

This is the deal I would pick for someone starting a Linux career. The LFCS + THRIVE-ONE bundle gets you the Linux Foundation Certified System Administrator exam along with a full year of the THRIVE-ONE e-learning subscription.

The LFCS exam itself is 65% off, so you pay $156 for the exam and $360 for the subscription. You save $109 over the regular bundle price, and $289 compared to buying both separately. No code is needed here, the discount is applied at checkout.

The subscription includes Linux System Administration Essentials (LFS207), the course built for LFCS preparation, along with 65+ other courses. So you get the study material and the exam in one go.

Get LFCS + THRIVE-ONE Bundle

The same 65% offer is available for other certifications too, including CKA, CKAD, CKS and KCNA. Look for the Cert + Subscription Bundles section on the promo page.

💡

FYI, I have registered for this exam. Not that I am looking for a job. I just want to fill the knowledge gap and test it. It may also give me ideas on creating courses focused on the certifications.

Linux Foundation Certified System Administrator (LFCS): $445 $223

If you only want the exam, LFCS is 50% off with the code BFCM26CCFOSS. You save $222.

LFCS is a 2-hour, performance-based exam. You work on a live Linux system from the command line and handle real tasks: networking, storage with LVM, users and groups, services, containers and SELinux. It is not tied to one distribution, and there are no prerequisites.

You also get two sessions on the Killer.sh exam simulator. The certification is valid for 2 years.

Get LFCS

CKA + CKAD + CKS Exam Bundle: $1,245 $498

Kubernetes skills are what most cloud and DevOps job listings ask for. This bundle groups the three professional Kubernetes certifications: Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA), Certified Kubernetes Application Developer (CKAD) and Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist (CKS).

At 60% off, you save $747. That works out to $166 per exam, which is less than the discounted price of a single exam on its own.

All three are 2-hour, performance-based exams on live Kubernetes clusters, with Killer.sh simulator access. Keep in mind that you must pass CKA before you can take CKS.

Get CKA + CKAD + CKS Bundle

If you want CKA and CKAD with their companion courses, the Power Bundle for both is $516 instead of $1,290 with the code BFCM26PBUNFOSS.

Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA): $445 $223

If you want to start with just one Kubernetes exam, make it CKA. It is the most widely recognized Kubernetes certification and the one that cloud and DevOps job listings mention the most. You save $222 with the code BFCM26CCFOSS.

CKA is a 2-hour, performance-based exam where you set up, manage and troubleshoot a live Kubernetes cluster from the command line. There are no prerequisites, and it includes two Killer.sh simulator sessions and one retake.

It also unlocks CKS later, as CKA is a prerequisite for it.

Get CKA

Kubestronaut Bundle: $1,995 $998

This one is for people who want to go all in on cloud native. The Kubestronaut bundle includes six certification exams: KCNA, KCSA, CKA, CKAD, CKS and the new CKNE.

KCNA and KCSA are beginner-friendly multiple choice exams. The other four are hands-on, performance-based exams. You save $997, which is half the regular price.

It is a big commitment, but you have 12 months to work through the exams.

Get Kubestronaut Bundle

If you already have CKA or CKAD, there are upgrade bundles at $823 on the promo page, so you don't pay for an exam you have already cleared.

THRIVE-ONE Annual (e-learning): $360 $252

THRIVE-ONE is the Linux Foundation's training subscription. The annual plan gives you unlimited access to the entire e-learning catalog for a year, plus all SkillCred exams (not the certification exams).

You also get a 40% coupon for any certification or course and 50% off guaranteed-to-run instructor-led courses. Note that certification exams are not included in the subscription.

This works well if you want to learn several technologies over the year before deciding which exam to take. The 30% discount applies to the first year of new subscriptions. The monthly plan is also 30% off, $25 instead of $35, for the first three months.

Get THRIVE-ONE Annual

MCPA + AGNTCon Event Pass: $650 $399

If you are into AI agents, there is a new bundle that pairs the Model Context Protocol Associate (MCPA) certification exam with a pass to AGNTCon + MCPCon, happening April 28 to 29, 2027, in San Francisco. With the code BFCM26MCPAGNTFOSS, you pay $399 for both instead of $650. The exam itself is 60% off and the event pass is $100 off.

You get access to the MCPA exam immediately. The event voucher and registration instructions will be emailed by December 15, 2026.

Get MCPA + Event Pass Bundle

Exams are online, with a free retake and a money back guarantee

A few things that make this deal more lucrative.

The exams are online. They are remotely proctored, so you can take them from home on your own computer. No need to travel to a test center.

You don't have to take the exam this week. You only need to buy before December 4. Linux Foundation certifications come with 12 months of exam eligibility, so you can lock in the discounted price now and prepare at your own pace.

You get a free retake. LFCS, CKA, CKAD, CKS and most other certifications include one retake. If your first attempt does not go well, you get a second chance without paying again but within one year of your purchase. That's a big relief, in my opinion.

There is a money-back guarantee. You can request a refund of the exam fee within 3 business days of purchase, as long as you have not scheduled the exam yet. For courses, it is 3 business days and the course should not be completed. Please read the policy here.

Why get certified at all?

A certification is a way to prove to a recruiter that you have the skill. Anyone can list "Kubernetes" or "Linux administration" on a resume. A certification from the Linux Foundation tells the hiring manager that someone has actually tested you on it.

This matters even more for performance-based exams like CKA and LFCS where you don't pick answers from a list. You fix real problems on a live system within a time limit, which is pretty much what the job looks like.

Certifications are even more helpful if you are a fresh graduate, or if you are switching to a new domain like cloud or DevOps.

And it is not just my opinion. In the Linux Foundation's 2026 State of Tech Talent report, 76% of organizations said they value certifications when assessing candidates for a technical role. That is slightly ahead of college degrees at 74%, and this is the third year in a row that certifications have ranked above degrees.

Offer ends on 4th December so make a decision now. Getting certified could also be your new year resolution.

items.title: Signal Takes a Radical Step to Block Gemini and Siri From Reading Your Chats
items.summary: Signal wants Apple and Google to give apps an easy way to opt out of AI data access.
items.body:
Using a privacy-focused messenger like Signal is a good idea, but AI assistants now baked into recent smartphones, such as Google's Gemini and Apple's Siri, can read whatever is showing on the screen.

The president of the Signal Foundation, Meredith Whittaker, says this leaves the messaging app between a rock and a hard place, as operating system makers have not given apps good ways to block AI access to their data.

This leaves Signal to make do with the tools it has. Its open source code and encryption protocol have backed its privacy promise for over a decade, but neither helps once the operating system starts capturing the screen.

Whatever the assistant picks up gets stored, and where it ends up is down to the OS agent, be it a local database or a remote server. Signal has no control over that.

The risks

AI agents in the OS, capturing sensitive data from apps like Signal, present an existential threat to privacy

Sadly, OS vendors are integrating agents recklessly, w/o giving Signal and other apps good ways to block AI data access and protect you

So, we're doing what we can w/… https://t.co/R1Ls2zOu1L

Your phone is not the only one that matters. A chat shows up on every participant's screen, and Signal says an assistant reading any one of them can potentially expose everyone in the conversation.

On Android, the answer is to turn on Screen security automatically the first time an AI assistant tries to read Signal's screen. This needs you to be on Signal 8.35.1 or later.

The app relies on detection because Android differs from vendor to vendor, and many phones give it no reliable way to spot a screenshot attempt once screenshots are blocked.

Not every Android phone gets this protection because it depends on Signal being able to notice an assistant at work.

On iPhones running iOS 27 and Signal 8.37 or later, a new "Block Siri AI" setting is enabled by default. It blocks screenshots and screen recordings inside the app and hides the app from the App Switcher.

Anyone who tries a screenshot gets a message with several choices, and the setting can be switched off entirely or for 10 minutes only.

Signal calls the fix incomplete because content can still be pulled from the filesystem, and turning the protection off can potentially expose your content and your contacts' content too.

Macs are left out as well. Signal says macOS offers no way to restrict AI access without a major hit to the user experience, and that is why the protection is missing there for now.

Signal wants a developer opt-out

Signal first tried this on Windows 11 last year, when it used screenshot blocking to keep Recall away from chats.

Its ask has not changed since. Signal wants Apple, Google, and Microsoft to give developers an easy, documented way to opt apps out of AI data access, along with better documentation of how these agents work.

It says it is hopeful, with some caution, about its talks with Google and Apple.

Interestingly, users do have some controls of their own. The EFF says that iOS 27.2 added an "Excluded Apps" list that stops Siri AI from reading any app on it.

What stands out to me is how little control an app has over this. Signal can block screenshots and watch for assistants on some Android versions, but the outcome still depends on each person's phone, OS version, and settings.

That matters in a conversation with several people, since one person switching the protection off can potentially expose the rest.

translation.title: Signal采取激进措施阻止Gemini和Siri读取你的聊天记录
translation.summary: Signal 希望苹果和谷歌为应用提供一种简单的方式来退出 AI 数据访问。
translation.label: 机器翻译
translation.summary_source: Signal wants Apple and Google to give apps an easy way to opt out of AI data access.
translation.body:
使用像 Signal 这样注重隐私的通讯应用是个好主意，但如今内置在近期智能手机中的 AI 助手，例如谷歌的 Gemini 和苹果的 Siri，能够读取屏幕上显示的任何内容。

Signal 基金会主席梅雷迪思·惠特克表示，这让这款通讯应用陷入进退两难的境地，因为操作系统厂商没有为应用提供阻止 AI 访问其数据的良好方式。

这迫使 Signal 只能利用现有工具勉强应对。其开源代码和加密协议十多年来一直支撑着它的隐私承诺，但一旦操作系统开始截取屏幕，这两者都无济于事。

助手抓取到的任何内容都会被存储，而最终存于何处取决于操作系统的代理程序，可能是本地数据库，也可能是远程服务器。Signal 对此无法控制。

风险

操作系统中的 AI 代理从 Signal 等应用抓取敏感数据，对隐私构成生存性威胁

遗憾的是，操作系统厂商正在鲁莽地集成代理程序，没有为 Signal 和其他应用提供阻止 AI 数据访问并保护你的良好方式

因此，我们正在尽我们所能…… https://t.co/R1Ls2zOu1L

你的手机并不是唯一重要的。聊天会出现在每个参与者的屏幕上，Signal 表示，助手读取其中任何一人的屏幕，都可能暴露对话中的所有人。

在 Android 上，解决办法是在 AI 助手首次尝试读取 Signal 屏幕时自动开启屏幕安全保护。这需要你使用 Signal 8.35.1 或更高版本。

该应用依赖检测来实现这一点，因为 Android 各厂商版本不尽相同，而且许多手机在截图被阻止后，无法可靠地识别截图尝试。

并非每部 Android 手机都能获得这一保护，因为这取决于 Signal 能否察觉到助手正在运行。

在运行 iOS 27 和 Signal 8.37 或更高版本的 iPhone 上，新增的“阻止 Siri AI”设置默认启用。它会阻止应用内的截图和屏幕录制，并在应用切换器中隐藏该应用。

任何尝试截图的人都会收到一条包含多个选项的提示，该设置可以完全关闭，也可以仅关闭 10 分钟。

Signal 称这一修复并不完整，因为内容仍可从文件系统中提取，而且关闭保护可能会暴露你的内容以及你联系人的内容。

Mac 也被排除在外。Signal 表示，macOS 没有提供在不严重损害用户体验的情况下限制 AI 访问的方法，这就是目前该平台缺少这一保护的原因。

Signal 希望开发者能选择退出

Signal 去年首次在 Windows 11 上尝试了这一做法，当时它利用截图阻止功能让 Recall 无法访问聊天内容。

自那以后，它的诉求没有改变。Signal 希望苹果、谷歌和微软为开发者提供一种简单且有文档记录的方式，让应用选择退出 AI 数据访问，同时提供关于这些代理程序运作方式的更完善文档。

有趣的是，用户自己确实有一些控制手段。电子前沿基金会表示，iOS 27.2 新增了“排除的应用”列表，可阻止 Siri AI 读取列表中的任何应用。

Happy Thanksgiving from It's FOSS 🦃

items.title: Quoth: A Local AI Speech to Text Tool for Linux That Picks Your Hardware
items.summary: Quoth is a new open source dictation app made only for Linux. It runs Whisper AI models locally and benchmarks your CPU, GPU and NPU to pick the fastest one. Pretty good tool actually.
items.body:
I keep testing voice typing tools on Linux, and most of them do the job. The annoying part is figuring out which model your computer can actually handle, and whether it should run on the CPU, the GPU or the NPU.

Quoth does that part for you. It's a new voice dictation app made exclsuively for Linux. It runs Whisper models locally, and it benchmarks your hardware to decide what runs where.

I tried it on my Ubuntu with GNOME and I am sharing my experience in this article. I have also recorded it in video format, but there is construction work going on in the neighborhood, so the voiceover recording is postponed. Hopefully, I will share the video in a few days. For now, read and enjoy 😄

What is Quoth?

Quoth is a local AI, speech to text tool. You press a key, you speak, and your words get typed wherever your mouse cursor is. That could be a text editor, a browser, a chat app or even the terminal (although command typing is more miss than hit).

Everything is transcribed on your own machine with whisper.cpp. There's no need and scope for account creation. You can choose to share crash reports with dev, if you want to. It's disabled by default. Quoth says the reports never contain your audio or dictated text.

Here's a quick summary of what Quoth offers:

• Four Whisper models: Tiny, Base, Small and Turbo (large-v3-turbo)

• Hardware acceleration on Vulkan GPUs (AMD, Intel and NVIDIA) and Intel NPUs through OpenVINO

• A built-in benchmark that picks the fastest device (CPU, GPU or NPU) for each model

• Tap to talk or hold to talk modes

• Translation from 10+ languages into English (except with Turbo)

• Addition themes like Nord, Catppuccin and Dracula

It's free and open source under the GPL-3.0 license, and it's built by a single developer, Samuel Bullard. Samuel gave me an early access to the tool for trying out. It is available to public now.

For now, you need Wayland, as X11 is not supported. And you need a 64-bit x86 machine, as there are no ARM builds yet.

Installing Quoth

Quoth offers a deb package (recommended for Ubuntu 24.04 and Pop!_OS 24.04), an APT repository if you want automatic updates, and a Flatpak bundle. Arch users can build it with the PKGBUILD in the repository. It's not on Flathub or the AUR yet.

The install page on the Quoth website has the exact commands for each method. I used the deb package on Ubuntu.

One thing for GNOME users: Quoth lives in the top panel as a tray icon, so you need an AppIndicator extension. Ubuntu ships one by default. On vanilla GNOME, you'll have to install it yourself.

First run and setup

On the first run, Quoth downloads the Base model. It's only 82 MB, so this takes a few seconds or minutes, depending on the internet connection. Then it asks you to try your voice.

I said "I love private, local and open source transcription" and it got every word right. Then I tried something it was less likely to know: "Everyone should subscribe to It's FOSS YouTube channel." It got itsfoss.com correct, but It's FOSS became "its Forest". That's acceptable for such a small model, I think.

The benchmark is the best part

This is perhaps the most unique feature. Quoth offers to benchmark the model on your NPU, GPU and CPU. After that, its automatic mode picks the fastest device on its own.

On my laptop, Asus Zenbook, the GPU came out on top at 22 times real time. That means it can transcribe 22 seconds of speech in one second. I didn't have to guess anything, and that's what I like most about Quoth.

First hiccup: one key shortcut only

Quoth then asks you to choose a dictation key. The default is Pause, and I wanted something else, like Ctrl+Alt+Space.

That didn't work. When I pressed the combination, Quoth only registered the Control key. You can set a single key, not a combination.

Quoth does warn you that Ctrl is a modifier key, so dictation would start every time you use it in a shortcut. I went with the Home key instead, because I use it less than other keys. But a single key is never ideal, because that key still does its normal job in other apps.

Dictating with Quoth in everyday apps

Once set up, Quoth sits in the top panel. The icon turns red/orange while it's recording. Unlike Ubuntu's Myna, it doesn't show a pill or some other visual feedback that recording is in progress. It does have a small audio feedback when dictation starts.

In a text editor

I opened Gedit text editor, pressed Home, spoke, and pressed Home again. The text appeared at my cursor.

The Base model wrote "It's forz.com" this time. But the rest of the sentence was correct, even with my accent. Later, I tried the same kind of sentence with the Turbo model, and it got "itsfoss.com" right (the last line in the screenshot above).

In the terminal

Quoth does paste in the terminal. But "sudo apt update" became "sudo app update", twice.

So I wouldn't use it for commands. To be fair, that's true for every dictation tool I've tried. Commands are short, and typing them is faster anyway, and safer too.

In chat and AI prompts

For casual chat on Discord, it works well as hort sentences come out right. I think chats are one of the best places to use the speech to text tools.

Speech to text in Discord

Another place where I find dictation most useful is for creating long prompts for AI tools. I asked Lumo AI from Proton to go through my Proton Mail inbox (connected via Proton Bridge) and find software coverage requests in the past 24 hours. Quoth misheard Proton as "Praton" (did I speak that badly?), but Lumo understood the request anyway and correctly listed six requests.

Used Quoth in Proton Lumo AI desktop app

Speaking a long prompt is much faster than typing it, and small errors don't matter much because the AI model works around them.

Click the Quoth icon in the top panel and you get a small menu. It has Language and Model options, along with Copy last dictation, Settings, About and Quit.

Clicking on Language and Model could not open a submenu. I had to go to Settings to change either of them. This is a bug and I have notified Samuel about it. Hopefully he will take care of it in the next update.

Exploring the settings

Quoth interface is clean, uses libadwaita, and blends well with GNOME.

In the Dictation tab, you can switch between tap to start and stop, or hold while you talk. You also pick your model here.

Model

Download size

Translation to English

Tiny

44 MB

Yes

Base

82 MB

Yes

Small

264 MB

Yes

Turbo

874 MB

No

Even the largest model is under 1 GB. That's small compared to what other tools offer. Keep in mind that if you use the NPU, Quoth downloads an extra encoder for it. When I downloaded Turbo, the download was 1.3 GB (because of the encoder), and the NPU cache took 1.4 GB on disk afterwards.

You can also set the language you speak and turn on translation to English. The Feedback tab has recording sounds, the volume for them, and notifications while recording.

The Performance tab lets you force the NPU, GPU or CPU if you don't like the automatic choice, or run the benchmark again.

There's also an option to keep the model loaded in memory. By default, it stays loaded for 300 seconds after your last dictation. That uses more RAM, but you get a faster response.

In the General tab, you can change the app skin. The themes change the colors of the settings window, and I quite like the Catppuccin one.

Running the full benchmark

After downloading Turbo, I ran the benchmark again from settings. This time it tested both models.

For the Base model, my laptop managed 15 times real time on the NPU, 23 on the GPU and 5.6 on the CPU. Turbo took much longer to test.

The final results surprised me. Base is fastest on the GPU at 23 times real time. But Turbo is fastest on the NPU, at 4.8 times real time.

I wouldn't have guessed that. And when I switched to Turbo, the automatic mode moved to the NPU on its own. This is exactly the kind of decision most of us would not make on our own.

Testing Turbo model

blocks.text: I keep testing voice typing tools on Linux, and most of them do the job. The annoying part is figuring out which model your computer can actually handle, and whether it should run on the CPU, the GPU or the NPU.
Quoth does that part for you. It's a new voice dictation app made exclsuively for Linux. It runs Whisper models locally, and it benchmarks your hardware to decide what runs where.

I tried it on my Ubuntu with GNOME and I am sharing my experience in this article. I have also recorded it in video format, but there is construction work going on in the neighborhood, so the voiceover recording is postponed. Hopefully, I will share the video in a few days. For now, read and enjoy 😄
What is Quoth?

Quoth is a local AI, speech to text tool. You press a key, you speak, and your words get typed wherever your mouse cursor is. That could be a text editor, a browser, a chat app or even the terminal (although command typing is more miss than hit).

Everything is transcribed on your own machine with whisper.cpp. There's no need and scope for account creation. You can choose to share crash reports with dev, if you want to. It's disabled by default. Quoth says the reports never contain your audio or dictated text.

Hardware acceleration on Vulkan GPUs (AMD, Intel and NVIDIA) and Intel NPUs through OpenVINO
A built-in benchmark that picks the fastest device (CPU, GPU or NPU) for each model

Addition themes like Nord, Catppuccin and Dracula

blocks.text: It's free and open source under the GPL-3.0 license, and it's built by a single developer, Samuel Bullard. Samuel gave me an early access to the tool for trying out. It is available to public now.
For now, you need Wayland, as X11 is not supported. And you need a 64-bit x86 machine, as there are no ARM builds yet.
Installing Quoth

Quoth offers a deb package (recommended for Ubuntu 24.04 and Pop!_OS 24.04), an APT repository if you want automatic updates, and a Flatpak bundle. Arch users can build it with the PKGBUILD in the repository. It's not on Flathub or the AUR yet.
The install page on the Quoth website has the exact commands for each method. I used the deb package on Ubuntu.
One thing for GNOME users: Quoth lives in the top panel as a tray icon, so you need an AppIndicator extension. Ubuntu ships one by default. On vanilla GNOME, you'll have to install it yourself.

This is perhaps the most unique feature. Quoth offers to benchmark the model on your NPU, GPU and CPU. After that, its automatic mode picks the fastest device on its own.

blocks.text: On my laptop, Asus Zenbook, the GPU came out on top at 22 times real time. That means it can transcribe 22 seconds of speech in one second. I didn't have to guess anything, and that's what I like most about Quoth.

blocks.alt: Quoth registers only Ctrl when trying to set a key combination

blocks.text: Quoth does warn you that Ctrl is a modifier key, so dictation would start every time you use it in a shortcut. I went with the Home key instead, because I use it less than other keys. But a single key is never ideal, because that key still does its normal job in other apps.

blocks.alt: Text dictated with Quoth in a text editor

blocks.text: The Base model wrote "It's forz.com" this time. But the rest of the sentence was correct, even with my accent. Later, I tried the same kind of sentence with the Turbo model, and it got "itsfoss.com" right (the last line in the screenshot above).
In the terminal

blocks.alt: Quoth dictation in the terminal turns apt into app

blocks.text: So I wouldn't use it for commands. To be fair, that's true for every dictation tool I've tried. Commands are short, and typing them is faster anyway, and safer too.

items.title: Linus Torvalds is Angry Again, This Time With ext4 Dev
items.summary: "You are full of crap". Linux creator Linus Torvalds gets angry at ext4 maintainer.
items.body:
Theodore Ts'o, who maintains ext4, sent Linus Torvalds a pull request of 94 commits for Linux 7.4-rc5, and the merge commit that followed adds 41,204 lines across 68 files.

Ts'o said KUnit tests make up most of the added code and exist to help validate patches that AI generates, and that most of the bug fixes in the pull were AI generated as well.

What was in the pull that got Torvalds all worked up?

Before we dive into that, know that the ext4 filesystem grew out of ext3 and was built to be reliable and to scale to large storage, including filesystems larger than 16TB.

Whereas KUnit is the kernel's unit testing framework, where tests are written in C and run against kernel code at boot or as a module.

The tests in Ts'o's pull account for 22 of the 68 changed files in the merge commit. The rest is bug fixes and three minor performance changes.

One performance change spreads the inodes of files in sibling directories over a flex group's block groups and speeds up parallel file creation. Another moves the orphan list fields off a shared cache line, and a third skips holes when replaying fast commits for sparse files.

The bug fixes include data loss cases, such as fsync'ed data lost after a journal flush and data lost during ext3 inode migration.

Others cover stale data after a failed zeroout, use-after-free bugs, out-of-bounds accesses on corrupted filesystems and a readdir problem with large directories on 32-bit kernels.

Torvalds objected to 41,197 lines of code being added so late in release cycle

Kernel development works in cycles, with new code going in during a merge window of about two weeks. The weekly release candidates that follow, called "rc" builds, are meant for fixes, and a cycle usually reaches somewhere between rc6 and rc9.

Torvalds objected that a pull of this size belongs in the merge window and that calling something a fix does not make it fit for an rc.

He said more than 41,000 added lines can cause new problems even when most of them are tests or fixes for other bugs. Fixes for old, subtle bugs can bring bugs of their own too, whether a person or an AI wrote them.

He took the pull after thinking about dropping it, and he closed his reply with a warning to Ts'o:

Get your shit together and stop this kind of
idiocy.

And tell your AI companion to get its act together, and do any new development and test-cases ON A SEPARATE DAMN BRANCH, so that it can be merged during the MERGE WINDOW.

What's so hard to understand about this?

How it ended

Ts'o replied that the tests were already on their own branch and had been placed at the end of the pull so they could be dropped easily. He offered to send a new pull request without them and hold the tests back until the next merge window opened.

Torvalds answered that he still partly objected, but he kept the merge. The conflicts from the test changes were not enough to make him undo it.

What Linus has said before

Torvalds complained in May about a bloated rc with pointless pull requests, much of it AI assisted, and promised to be tougher. But he has also said Linux is not one of those anti-AI projects.

By his count, the 7.4 merge window brought almost 20,000 commits against the roughly 15,000 that is typical. He would rather get AI fixes there than late in an rc, and he hopes they become mundane.

内核开发按周期进行，新代码在约两周的合并窗口期间进入。随后的每周候选版本称为“rc”版本，用于修复，一个周期通常达到 rc6 到 rc9 之间。

Torvalds 反对说，这种规模的拉取请求应属于合并窗口，而且把某样东西称为修复并不能使其适合 rc。

他说，超过 41,000 行新增代码可能引发新问题，即使其中大部分是测试或其他缺陷的修复。对旧的、隐蔽缺陷的修复也可能带来自身的缺陷，无论作者是人还是 AI。

他在考虑放弃后还是接受了该拉取请求，并在回复结尾警告 Ts'o：

把你的烂摊子收拾好，别再干这种
蠢事。

还要告诉你的 AI 伙伴端正态度，任何新开发和测试用例都要放在一个单独的该死分支上，以便能在合并窗口期间合并。

这有什么难理解的？

结局如何

Ts'o 回复说，测试已经放在单独分支上，并被放在拉取请求末尾以便轻松丢弃。他提出可以发送一个不含这些测试的新拉取请求，并将测试推迟到下一个合并窗口开启。

Torvalds 回答说，他仍部分反对，但他保留了这次合并。测试变更引发的冲突不足以让他撤销合并。

Linus 此前说过什么

Torvalds 在 5 月曾抱怨一个臃肿的 rc 包含无意义的拉取请求，其中很多是 AI 辅助的，并承诺会更严格。但他也表示 Linux 不属于那些反 AI 的项目。

据他统计，7.4 合并窗口带来了近 20,000 个提交，而通常约为 15,000 个。他更愿意在那里收到 AI 修复，而不是在 rc 后期，并希望它们变得司空见惯。

items.title: Meet Warty, the AI Launcher Canonical Is Building for Ubuntu
items.summary: Ubuntu's AI launcher should be available in January. Every AI feature introduced is being strictly opt-in and local-first.
items.body:
Back in April, Canonical shared its plans for AI in Ubuntu, favoring models that run on the user's own hardware and open-weight options over cloud services.

The plan also split AI features as behind-the-scenes improvements to existing parts of the OS and visible, as well as agentic ones that users opt into.

Myna came next, a speech-to-text tool that runs on local models. It debuted as an optional preview in Ubuntu 26.10, and the company says it will ship by default with Ubuntu 28.04 LTS.

More recently, Canonical introduced Surge at Ubuntu Summit 26.10. The AI system writes and checks security fixes for Ubuntu packages, and those fixes are offered through an opt-in archive for Ubuntu Pro users instead of reaching stable releases automatically.

Now the newest step in this direction is an AI-powered launcher.

It first showed up as a simulated snap on the Snap Store in October, and Didier Roche, the developer working on it, has now explained where the project is headed.

An AI-powered launcher?

Current status of Warty Launcher. (Source: Didier Roche)

The aim of this new launcher (warty-launcher) is to provide a single spot on the desktop for finding files, opening apps, and getting help from an AI model on request.

Both typing and talking are input types that are to be supported. ⌨️🗣️

Unlike the October prototype snap, the launcher now actually runs and has some functionality built into it, with Canonical publishing its technical design and first public release in January 2027.

Alongside that, testing also opens, and the developers are looking forward to collecting feedback on their design choices.

Didier also mentions that turning on AI is the user's choice, with the traditional app launcher staying the default experience for anyone who prefers it.

Additionally, large AI models will not come bundled with the default install for Warty Launcher.

Anyone who opts in is meant to get inference on their own machine ahead of remote servers, with personal files, session context, etc. not leaving the machine.

The parts that power it are built to stay isolated under Ubuntu's confinement tools to protect the host system.

However, the announcement does not name the models or the hardware requirements, and some foundational work still has to be finished first.

A brief demo

After launching the prototype Snap package for Warty Launcher, a small button appears at the top right of the screen inside the top panel with shortcuts for Clipboard, Emoji, Files, and Tasks.

If you remember from earlier, Didier's post shows a newer build that places the launcher near the top center instead; I prefer the newer approach.

The Clipboard mode lists recent copies with the app and time each one came from. The sample entries include a restaurant booking, a hotel address, and a train ticket screenshot, and a follow-up button next to the search field hands any of them to the AI.

The latest build of Warty Launcher. (Source: Diedier Roche)

Once I sent a test prompt through the follow-up, it showed a "Working on this device" message and then returned lorem ipsum filler as the answer. This was a given, as the Snap store listing for the prototype says actions are simulated.

Emoji shows a grid of recent picks. Files waits for three characters before it offers to open a match or show it in the file manager, and Tasks keeps a list of what the launcher has done, such as opening files.

Test it yourself

If you want to try it yourself, the snap is only available on the edge channel and installs via a single command:

sudo snap install warty-prototype --edge

Once it is installed, running warty-prototype in a terminal starts it and opens the launcher.

A few GTK and graphics warnings showed up in my terminal, but the launcher still appeared. To close it, pick "Quit the prototype" from the right-click menu in the top panel.

This is a standalone prototype with simulated actions and demo data. If you are hoping to use it, give it a few more weeks before it matures into a daily-use kind of feature.
